opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a pretty strong case for it, though I'd frame the appeal differently depending on who you're talking to.

From a purely intellectual standpoint, it's striking how much of our actual reasoning in math and science runs on arguments that aren't proofs. Think about the twin prime conjecture: we have a very convincing heuristic argument, basically treating primes as random with the right density, that predicts not just that there are infinitely many twin primes but roughly how many. Mathematicians mostly believe it, and they believe it because of that argument. Physicists do this constantly too, with dimensional analysis, perturbative expansions, and "assume these things are independent unless you have a reason to think they're correlated." Yet we don't have a good account of what makes these arguments valid, when they fail, or how to combine them. There's no notion of a heuristic argument analogous to what formal proof gives you for deduction. That seems like a pretty big hole.

For me, though, the real motivation is alignment. The problem I care about is something like: you have a neural network that behaves well on the training distribution, and you want to know *why* it behaves well. Is it because it's doing the thing you wanted, or because it's doing something else that happens to coincide on the inputs you checked? Proofs are hopeless here. You're never going to formally prove properties of a giant learned model. But "explanation" in the sense of a heuristic argument might be achievable. If you could produce something like "here's an argument for why this model's output has this property, and here's the structure of that argument," you could notice when the model is behaving well for an anomalous reason on some new input, even if you can't say exactly what the model is doing. That's the mechanistic anomaly detection angle, and it also bears on eliciting latent knowledge.

So the pitch is: interpretability tries to get humans to understand models, and that may not scale. If instead you had a formal notion of "an explanation for this behavior" that an algorithm could search for, the way we search for parameters with gradient descent, you could get some of the benefits of understanding without a human ever needing to understand.

I should be honest about the downsides. It's very ambitious, and it's quite possible there's no clean formalization. Heuristic reasoning might just be irreducibly messy, and you'd end up with something too weak to be useful or too ad hoc to be principled. It's also a weird bet sociologically. It doesn't look like normal ML research, and it doesn't look like normal math either, so it's hard to get feedback. My view is that the probability of success is low-ish but the payoff is large enough, and the work is neglected enough, that it's a reasonable thing for a small group to spend years on. And even partial progress, like being able to say precisely what it means for one argument to "explain away" a surprise, seems like it would teach us something.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the appeal is actually pretty strong, and it comes from a few different directions.

The first is just that this is something everyone does and nobody has a good account of. If you ask a mathematician why they believe the twin prime conjecture, they'll give you a heuristic argument: primes behave roughly like random numbers with density one over log n, so you'd expect about this many twin primes up to x, and that matches the data. That's not a proof. But it's also not nothing. It's a kind of reasoning that moves credences a lot, and mathematicians are pretty good at it. Physicists do the same thing constantly, with non-rigorous arguments about path integrals or renormalization that work shockingly well. In computer science you've got average-case analyses and random-oracle-style arguments where you say "treat this hash function as if it were random." In all these cases there's an implicit claim like "I don't see any structure that would make this thing deviate from the default," and then you reason as if there's no structure.

So the first appeal is just intellectual: there's clearly a real phenomenon here, it seems quite unified across fields, and we don't have a formal account of what makes these arguments good or when they fail. That feels like the kind of thing where there might actually be a theory to find.

The second thing, and this is why I personally care about it, is that it connects to alignment. The way I think about it, if you train a neural network and it does something, you'd like to be able to explain why it does that thing. Formal proofs about neural networks are hopeless. Even very simple properties aren't going to be provable in any reasonable sense. But heuristic arguments might be tractable. You might be able to say "here's a sketch of why this network outputs this on this distribution, and here's the presumption of independence I'm relying on." And then the interesting question becomes: can you detect when a model's behavior on some input is not explained by your argument? That's the kind of anomaly detection that could tell you a model is doing something unexpected before it actually matters.

The third appeal is more aesthetic, which is that it's a problem where the empirical constraints are pretty rich. You have thousands of existing heuristic arguments across these fields that your framework should either reproduce or explain why they're wrong. And you have cases where the heuristic was badly off, which are the most informative. So it's not like you're just making up definitions in a vacuum.

I'd also say I'm pretty uncertain whether it works out. It might be that the right notion of "heuristic argument" is irreducibly informal, or that any formalization is so weak that it doesn't capture the interesting cases. But I think the expected value of trying is high because the upside is big and the problem is pretty neglected relative to how fundamental it seems.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very appealing problem. We routinely have arguments that aren’t proofs, but that seem to give us good reasons to believe something. You see this in mathematics when people estimate how often some number-theoretic phenomenon should occur, or in computer science when they reason about how an algorithm will behave on typical inputs. And we don’t have a very satisfying general account of what makes those arguments good.

The interesting thing is that you’re often reasoning about uncertainty that comes from your own computational limitations. The answer is already determined by the definition of the problem. But you can’t compute it, so you treat parts of it as random. Then the question is: which parts can you legitimately treat as random, and which dependencies do you need to keep track of? If you get that wrong, you can produce very convincing arguments for false conclusions.

I’d be excited about a framework that made those choices explicit, so you could understand what assumptions an argument was making and how to improve it when it failed. I’m less sure that there’s one clean framework that captures everything people do. There’s a danger of writing down something sufficiently general that it doesn’t actually help you reason about any particular case. So I’d want to start with concrete examples where we understand why one heuristic works and another doesn’t, and see whether the same principles keep showing up.

sol-6.1.text:
I find it pretty appealing. In mathematics and computer science, we have a very good framework for talking about proofs, but a lot of our actual reasoning happens before we have a proof. We have intuitions about which approaches are likely to work, which patterns are meaningful, and when we should be surprised. And we don’t have a comparably good account of what makes those judgments reasonable.

You could imagine a framework that lets you say, “Here are the assumptions implicit in this heuristic, and here’s why this conclusion should follow approximately.” That would be useful both for understanding how humans reason and for building AI systems whose reasoning we can understand and evaluate.

The thing that makes me hesitant is that it’s easy to write down something that sounds like a general theory but doesn’t actually help you with any particular problem. So I’d want to start with concrete examples where people agree that a heuristic is compelling, even though they can’t turn it into a proof, and see whether you can explain what’s going on. If the same ideas keep working across different examples, then I’d start to get excited about a unifying framework.
